newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbekistan rejects IMF call on currency control.
newsitem.headline: Uzbekistan rejects IMF call on currency control.

text.p: Uzbek President Islam Karimov hit out angrily on Friday at pressure from international creditors who want the country's former Soviet-era leader to relax foreign exchange controls in return for loans.
Last week, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) suspended a $185 million standby loan to Tashkent, citing concern at currency controls and a failure to meet inflation targets.

But Karimov told reporters and diplomats that the Central Asian state had no need to make its sum currency fully convertible and accused the IMF of forcing countries which accepted loans to stabilise their currencies into "slavery".
The prevalence of black market money changers on the streets of the old Silk Road city of Tashkent, however, tells a different story of traders' demand for convertible currency.

Olya, in a smart raincoat and clutching a purse full of sums on the street, was breaking the law on Friday. She is one of many money changers who run the gauntlet of the police to trade the Uzbek currency for dollars, German marks or even Russian roubles in defiance of strict exchange control rules.
Standing on Amir Timur Street near the Alaisky Bazaar on a grey winter's day, Olya tried to catch the eyes of potential clients as they strolled past.
A few yards down the street, a bored-looking police officer sat in a jeep while young Uzbek men with hunted faces and leather jackets also hustled for gold and dollars.
"It's dangerous," said Olya, who saw colleagues carted off to prison for dealing on the black market earlier this year.

"But the police also don't earn much and have to feed their families," she said in reference to the "on the spot" fines -- in other words bribes -- the police usually extract when the black marketeers are caught red-handed.
In recent weeks, the spread between the official and black market rates has increased dramatically -- a dollar which bought 54.5 sums officially on Friday, was worth 114 on the street.
But Karimov thumbed his nose at the IMF and put paid to rumours swirling like old leaves down Amir Timur Street that full convertibility would be introduced next month.
"Our currency reserves have a duty to bring modern technology into the country," he said. Karimov wants hard currency to go on new technology, not "foreign chewing gum".
He said large investors, like gold mining companies, had "no problem" with convertibility and said he hoped he would find accord with an IMF mission due to visit at the end of January.
But he dismissed the suspended loan as a paltry sum and said: "The loans other countries have taken to stabilise their currencies have brought them into slavery."
Karimov, the country's communist boss in Soviet times, enjoys strong executive powers and tolerates little dissent. He believes economic reforms should be state led.
But the currency crisis has seen traders close their shops or withold goods in the largely desert nation of 23 million.
"Not for sale," said a salesman of a row of imported television sets at his electronics shop in central Tashkent.
Shops are suffering because they are forced by law to sell goods at the official -- and unprofitable -- rate of exchange.
So, despite the omnipresent Uzbek police, the black marketeers were busy on Friday. "They are rushing to buy presents for the New Year celebrations," Olya explained.
